# Capstone: a production decision service {#sec-ch21}

::: {.epigraph by="A saying among site reliability engineers"}
Hope is not a strategy.
:::

Every project reaches the moment when the prototype works and someone asks: "Great. Can we run it on Monday?"

That's harder than anything in the prototype. A model that decides well on a laptop is not a service. A service answers at three in the morning when the API is slow, explains itself to an auditor a year later, tells someone when the world has changed, and changes safely when you improve it. This chapter assembles one from pieces built across the book.

::: {.goals}
- Put everything that changes a decision into one versioned config, and stamp every decision with it.
- Design a decision record that answers "why?" a year later.
- Give every failure a decided meaning, and test it by making calls fail on purpose.
- Monitor a decision service with a handful of numbers that raise flags a person reads.
- Try a new version in shadow before it touches anything.
:::

## The shape of the service

![The decision service. Each alert's trusted fields go to Jev as three typed questions; the answer is calibrated, and the policy, business rules and capacity turn it into a zone. Every decision is recorded before it is returned. Any failure falls back to review. A daily monitor reads the log, and a candidate version can run in shadow beside the current one.](/figures/ch28/architecture.pdf){#fig-architecture-21}

You'll recognise every box in @fig-architecture-21. The input is built from trusted fields only, never free text an attacker could write (Chapter 7). The three typed questions are Chapter 10's. The calibration is Chapter 11's. The policy, with its capacity, is Chapter 14's. The rest is what turns a chain of steps into a service.

## One config, one fingerprint

The first rule is this:

::: {.keyidea}
Everything that can change a decision lives in one place, with a version number.
:::

The model version, the calibration numbers, the thresholds and every business rule ("never auto-close a critical system") live in one small configuration. Every decision is stamped with its version and a fingerprint that changes if anything in it changes. Why so strict? Because months later the question you'll hear most is "why did it do *that*?", and the answer depends on which settings were live that week.

## The decision record

Every call to the service returns, and logs, a record like this one.

![One decision record, with notes on why each field is there. Together they say what the service saw, what the model said, what the policy did, which version decided, and why.](/figures/ch28/record.pdf){#fig-record}

A decision model gives probabilities, not reasons. The answer for audits is to audit the *policy*, not the model. The record in @fig-record holds the raw and calibrated probabilities, the thresholds they met, the rule that fired and the version that decided. Together they explain every action in a way anyone can check, even though the model itself explains nothing.

::: {.keyidea}
You can't explain the model's probability, but you can make every action it led to fully explainable.
:::

## The dry run that found a bug

Before it touched anything, I ran the service over the live week as a "dry run", logging decisions without acting. The monitor flagged day one: the queue was over capacity. It shouldn't have been; the thresholds were fitted for 240 a day. But *after* fitting, someone had added a sensible rule: never auto-close an alert on a critical system. Every alert it moved from "act" to "review" was work the thresholds hadn't allowed for.

![Alerts sent to review each day of the live week, before and after the fix. Fitted without the critical-asset rule, the thresholds let the queue run over capacity every day. Fitted with it, the act threshold rises slightly and the queue fits.](/figures/ch28/dry-run.pdf){#fig-dry-run}

The fix: fit the thresholds *with* the rule in place. The act threshold moved from {{< num ch28 v1_low f3 >}} to {{< num ch28 v2_low f3 >}}, and the average queue went from about {{< num ch28 v1_mean_reviews int >}} to {{< num ch28 v2_mean_reviews int >}} a day (@fig-dry-run).

It's a small bug, and it's the most common kind: two reasonable changes, each tested alone, that don't work together. That's why the config holds the rules *and* the thresholds.

::: {.keyidea}
Thresholds and business rules are one decision, and they have to be fitted together.
:::

## When the call fails

The API will fail sometimes, and Chapter 16 said to decide in advance what failure *means*. Here it's a setting: a failed call sends the case to review.

![What happens to real threats when 10% of calls fail, under two fallbacks. Sending failures to review puts them in front of a person. Treating a failure as "act" would have closed them unseen, and nothing would have looked wrong.](/figures/ch28/failsafe.pdf){#fig-failsafe}

To test it, I made 10% of calls fail. With the fallback set to review, the {{< num ch28 fallback_threats int >}} real threats among the failed calls went to a person. With it set to "act", the same {{< num ch28 fallback_act_closed int >}} would have been closed without anyone seeing them. And every other number on the dashboard would have looked normal (@fig-failsafe). That's why the monitor watches the fallback rate: a failure you don't count is a failure you don't see.

::: {.keyidea}
Every failure needs a decided meaning, and the safe one puts a person in front of the case.
:::

## The monitor

Once a day, a small report reads the log and checks a few numbers against expected ranges: the share of cases in each zone, the queue against capacity, the fallback rate, and, for cases a person has seen, the share predicted real against the share confirmed real.

![Two weeks of the daily monitor: the live week, then the phishing campaign. Top: the review queue, red and striped on days a flag was raised. Bottom: for alerts people saw, the share the model predicted to be real against the share they confirmed. The campaign opens a gap on its first day.](/figures/ch28/monitor.pdf){#fig-monitor}

The quiet week raised no flags, which matters as much as what follows: people stop reading a monitor that cries wolf. On the campaign's first day, two flags went up: the queue was far over capacity, and the cases people saw were real far more often than predicted (@fig-monitor). That second flag is the one I'd most want in any decision service. It says, in plain numbers, *the probabilities are no longer calibrated*.

A flag only helps if someone reads it. So the service has a named owner with the authority to switch it to "review everything" while they find out what happened.

## Changing it safely

Every improvement (new calibration, thresholds, model version) is a new configuration, and it runs in **shadow mode** first: deciding every case beside the current version, logging what it would do, acting on nothing.

![A week of the candidate version in shadow beside the current one, in alerts per day. They agree on most alerts. The candidate would move about {{< num ch28 shadow_review_to_act_day int >}} alerts a day from review to auto-close: the gold cell, in the "current: review" row and the "new: act" column. That's the cell to look at before switching.](/figures/ch28/shadow.pdf){#fig-shadow-21}

The candidate here is the fixed config from the dry run. It agreed with the current version on {{< num ch28 shadow_agree pct >}} of alerts (@fig-shadow-21). The disagreements all go the same way. There are about {{< num ch28 shadow_review_to_act_day f1 >}} alerts a day that the current version sends to review and the candidate would close. Among those, about {{< num ch28 shadow_moved_threats_day f1 >}} a day were real threats.

That's the price of fitting the queue, not a bug, and the shadow run measures it before anyone pays it. Now someone can decide, with that number in front of them, whether to switch, hire, or accept an overflowing queue.

## The checklist

![Eight things a decision service needs before it runs on Monday.](/figures/ch28/checklist.pdf){#fig-checklist}

@fig-checklist is what I'd want done before switching on any decision service, whatever model is inside. None of it is specific to Jev; all of it is specific to *deciding*. Once a model's output closes a case, calls a person or blocks a login, every item stops being optional.

::: {.breaks}
This is a teaching service. A real one needs things this chapter leaves out. It needs sign-in for its callers and limits on how often they can call. It needs a proper log store rather than a file, and control over who can change the config. And it needs to protect the states it records, which may hold personal data. The monitor's expected ranges were set by eye from one quiet week, so treat them as a starting point to adjust. And shadow comparisons only show where versions *disagree*. If both versions are wrong in the same way, a shadow run can't tell you. Keep the random audit going.
:::

::: {.threshold}
To keep the queue at capacity, the candidate config in shadow would auto-close about 29 more alerts a day. About one of them is a real threat. A missed threat costs about \$10,000. An extra analyst costs about \$600 a day and clears 40 reviews. Should the company switch to the candidate, or keep the current version and add capacity?

(Switching saves about 29 reviews a day and costs about one missed threat, around \$10,000 a day in expected loss. Adding one analyst, at about \$600 a day, would handle those reviews instead. Unless hiring is impossible, keep the current thresholds and add capacity. The shadow run turned that from a guess into arithmetic.)
:::

Amazon's CTO Werner Vogels likes to say that everything fails, all the time. A decision service is built around that. Calls fail, models drift, campaigns arrive without warning. The service prevents none of it. It makes sure each failure has a decided meaning, leaves a record, and reaches a person who can act.

::: {.exercises}
1. Read a week of decision records and answer, from the log alone: which alert with P above 0.3 was auto-closed, and why?
2. Write one paragraph of instructions for the person who owns the flags: what they check first, and when they switch the service to review everything.
:::

::: {.nexthook}
Next: the last chapter. What changes, for the industry and for you, when deciding becomes cheap, fast and calibrated?
:::
